title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 23–27 (Night 232, continuing nights-231), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 232 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Bahādur, the king's master of the horse, finds al-Amjad and the young woman feasting in his hall; hearing that al-Amjad is a king's son, he takes pity on him and agrees to play his mamlūk, and al-Amjad must scold and beat him for coming late. The woman joins in the beating with a will, and at midnight, drunk, she demands that the sleeping slave be killed; rather than repay Bahādur's kindness with murder, al-Amjad cuts off her head instead. Bahādur carries the body off in a sack to throw it into the sea, but the governor's men surround him, find the dead woman, and bring him before the king, who takes him for a habitual murderer; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالثَّلٰثُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-thalāthūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and the thirty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and thirty-second night,
sentences.n: The night's opening formula: the unit, al-thāniyatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, all in the nominative with al-laylatu. thalāthūn is printed without its middle alif, والثلٰثون, with the dagger alif already set; the ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ بَهَادُرَ صَاحِبَ الْقَاعَةِ أَمِيرَ يَاخُورٍ لَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَى بَابِ الْقَاعَةِ وَرَأَى الْبَابَ مَفْتُوحًا فَدَخَلَ قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا وَطَلَّ بِرَأْسِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Bahādura ṣāḥiba al-qāʿati amīra yākhūrin lammā waṣala ilā bābi al-qāʿati wa-raʾā al-bāba maftūḥan fa-dakhala qalīlan qalīlan wa-ṭalla bi-raʾsihi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Bahādur, (the) owner (of) the-hall, commander (of the) stable, when he-arrived at (the) door (of) the-hall and-saw the-door open, then-he-entered little (by) little and-peeped with-his-head.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Bahādur, the owner of the hall and the king's master of the horse, came to the door of the hall and saw it standing open, he went in step by step and put his head round to look.
sentences.n: The night opens by retelling the last words of the night before, which broke off at fa-lammā waṣala ilā qarīb, 'when he drew near'. Here the print has plain lammā where the sense would lead one to expect fa-lammā, as there; it is kept. The answer to lammā is introduced by fa-, fa-dakhala, 'then he entered', which Classical Arabic would not use after lammā but Middle Arabic often does. amīr yākhūr, 'master of the horse', is vocalised as in the night before: a guess at a title the print spells ياخور for ākhūr. qalīlan qalīlan, 'little by little', cautiously. وطلّ is read ṭalla (its shadda is printed), the later and colloquial verb 'to look out, peep, put one's head out', and bi-raʾsihi, 'with his head', says how: he looked in by putting his head round the door. The hamza of رأى and of برأسه is printed.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ الْأَمْجَدَ وَالصَّبِيَّةَ وَقُدَّ امَهُمَا طَبَقُ الْفَاكِهَةِ وَالْجَرَّةُ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara al-Amjada wa-al-ṣabiyyata wa-quddāmahumā ṭabaqu al-fākihati wa-al-jarratu
sentences.l: And-he-saw al-Amjad and-the-girl, and-before-them-both (the) dish (of) the-fruit and-the-jar.
sentences.i: He saw al-Amjad and the girl, with the dish of fruit and the wine jar before them.
sentences.n: naẓara here takes its object directly, 'he saw', where Classical says naẓara ilā, 'looked at'; later Arabic often does this. The print sets وقدّامهما, 'and before them both', as two words, وقد امهما, as if wa-qad + something; it is kept as set and vocalised to show the one word quddāmahumā split in two. The clause wa-quddāmahumā … is circumstantial, 'with … before them'. The shadda of الجرّة is printed.

sentences.t: وَفِي ذٰلِكَ الْوَقْتِ كَانَ الْأَمْجَدُ مَاسِكَ الْقَدَحِ وَعَيْنُهُ إِلَى الْبَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī dhālika al-waqti kāna al-Amjadu māsika al-qadaḥi wa-ʿaynuhu ilā al-bābi
sentences.l: And-at that time was al-Amjad holding the-cup, and-his-eye to the-door.
sentences.i: At that moment al-Amjad was holding the cup, with his eye on the door.
sentences.n: māsika al-qadaḥi, 'holding the cup': masaka is the everyday later verb 'to hold', beside book Arabic amsaka; the participle is annexed to its object and stands as the predicate of kāna, so it is accusative. wa-ʿaynuhu ilā al-bābi is circumstantial, 'while his eye was on the door'. dhālika takes a dagger alif.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارَتْ عَيْنُهُ فِي عَيْنِ صَاحِبِ الدَّارِ اصْفَرَّ لَوْنُهُ وَارْتَعَدَتْ فَرَائِصُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣārat ʿaynuhu fī ʿayni ṣāḥibi al-dāri iṣfarra lawnuhu wa-irtaʿadat farāʾiṣuhu
sentences.l: And-when became his-eye in (the) eye (of the) owner (of) the-house, turned-yellow his-colour and-trembled his-shoulder-muscles.
sentences.i: When his eye met the eye of the master of the house, his colour drained away and he shook in every limb.
sentences.n: ṣārat ʿaynuhu fī ʿayni …, 'his eye came to be in the eye of …': their eyes met. iṣfarra, Form IX, 'to turn yellow', is the Arabic way of turning pale; its shadda is printed. farāʾiṣ, plural of farīṣa, the flesh between the shoulder and the breast, which quivers in a man who is afraid (Lane): irtaʿadat farāʾiṣuhu is the stock phrase for trembling with fear. The ئ is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُ بَهَادُرُ قَدِ اصْفَرَّ لَوْنُهُ وَتَغَيَّرَ حَالُهُ غَمَزَهُ بِإِصْبَعِهِ عَلَى فَمِهِ يَعْنِي اسْكُتْ وَتَعَالَ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu Bahāduru qadi iṣfarra lawnuhu wa-taghayyara ḥāluhu ghamazahu bi-iṣbaʿihi ʿalā famihi yaʿnī uskut wa-taʿāla ʿindī
sentences.l: And-when saw-him Bahādur (that) had turned-yellow his-colour and-changed his-state, he-signalled-to-him with-his-finger on his-mouth, meaning: Be-silent, and-come to-me.
sentences.i: When Bahādur saw that he had turned pale and was all undone, he signed to him with a finger on his lips, as if to say, “Hush, and come here to me.”
sentences.n: raʾāhu … qad iṣfarra, 'saw him (that) he had turned pale': the clause with qad says what he saw him to be. The madda of رآه and the shaddas of اصفرّ and تغيّر are printed. ghamaza, 'to signal (with the eye or the hand)', and bi-iṣbaʿihi, 'with his finger': bi- of the instrument. yaʿnī, 'it means', introduces what the gesture said. taʿāla, 'come!', and ʿindī, properly 'at my side', used after a verb of motion for 'to me', as later Arabic does.

sentences.t: فَحَطَّ الْأَمْجَدُ الْكَاسَ مِنْ يَدِهِ وَقَامَ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥaṭṭa al-Amjadu al-kāsa min yadihi wa-qāma ilayhi
sentences.l: And-put al-Amjad the-cup from his-hand and-rose to-him.
sentences.i: So al-Amjad set down the cup and got up to go to him.
sentences.n: ḥaṭṭa, properly 'to set down', the everyday later verb for 'to put'; its shadda is printed. al-kās is the spoken form of kaʾs, 'cup', its hamza softened; the print spells it so. qāma ilayhi, 'rose (and went) to him'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ إِلَى أَيْنَ فَحَرَّكَ رَأْسَهُ وَأَشَارَ لَهَا أَنَّهُ يُرِيقُ الْمَاءَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ṣabiyyatu ilā ayna fa-ḥarraka raʾsahu wa-ashāra lahā annahu yurīqu al-māʾa
sentences.l: And-said the-girl: To where? And-he-moved his-head and-signalled to-her that-he (is) pouring-out the-water.
sentences.i: “Where are you going?” said the girl. He gestured with his head and gave her to understand that he was going to make water.
sentences.n: ilā ayna, 'to where?', 'where are you off to?'. arāqa al-māʾa, 'to pour out water', is the polite phrase for passing water. ashāra lahā, 'he signalled to her': li- marks the one signalled to, where book Arabic has ilā. The shaddas of الصبيّة and حرّك and the hamza of رأسه are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَ إِلَى الدِّهْلِيزِ حَافِيًا
sentences.tr: thumma kharaja ilā al-dihlīzi ḥāfiyan
sentences.l: Then he-went-out to the-passage barefoot.
sentences.i: Then he went out barefoot into the passage.
sentences.n: ḥāfiyan, 'barefoot', a circumstantial accusative: he left his shoes behind, as one did on the carpets of a raised līwān. dihlīz, the entrance passage from the street door.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى بَهَادُرَ عَلِمَ أَنَّهُ صَاحِبُ الدَّارِ فَأَسْرَعَ إِلَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā Bahādura ʿalima annahu ṣāḥibu al-dāri fa-asraʿa ilayhi wa-qabbala yadayhi
sentences.l: And-when he-saw Bahādur, he-knew that-he (was the) owner (of) the-house, and-he-hastened to-him and-kissed his-two-hands.
sentences.i: When he saw Bahādur he knew that this was the master of the house, and he hurried to him and kissed his hands.
sentences.n: Bahādura is a diptote, so its accusative ends in -a without tanwīn. The hamza of رأى and the shadda of قبّل are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ بِاللّٰهِ عَلَيْكَ يَاسَيِّدِي قَبْلَ أَنْ تُؤْذِيَنِي أَنْ تَسْمَعَ مِنِّي مَقَالِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu bi-allāhi ʿalayka yā sayyidī qabla an tuʾdhiyanī an tasmaʿa minnī maqālī
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: By-God upon-you, O-my-lord, before that you-harm-me, that you-hear from-me my-saying.
sentences.i: “I beg you by God, my lord,” he said to him, “before you do me any harm, hear what I have to say.”
sentences.n: bi-allāhi ʿalayka, 'by God upon you', is an adjuration, 'I beg you by God'; what is begged follows as a bare an-clause, an tasmaʿa, 'that you hear', with the verb of asking left unsaid. maqāl, 'saying, what one has to say', a verbal noun of qāla: maqālī, 'my words'. The ؤ of تؤذيني is printed. The print runs yā sayyidī together, ياسيدي; kept as set.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَدَّثَهُ بِحَدِيثِهِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥaddathahu bi-ḥadīthihi min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi
sentences.l: Then he-told-him his-story from its-beginning to its-end.
sentences.i: Then he told him his story from beginning to end.
sentences.n: ḥaddatha bi-, 'to tell (someone) of': bi- marks the thing told. The shaddas of حدّثه and اوّله and the madda of آخره are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَخْبَرَهُ بِسَبَبِ خُرُوجِهِ مِنْ أَرْضِهِ وَمَمْلَكَتِهِ وَأَنَّهُ مَادَخَلَ الْقَاعَةَ بِاخْتِيَارِهِ وَلٰكِنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ هِيَ الَّتِي كَسَرَتِ الضَّبَّةَ وَفَتَحَتِ الْبَابَ وَفَعَلَتْ هٰذِهِ الْفِعَالَ
sentences.tr: wa-akhbarahu bi-sababi khurūjihi min arḍihi wa-mamlakatihi wa-annahu mā dakhala al-qāʿata bi-ikhtiyārihi wa-lākinna al-ṣabiyyata hiya allatī kasarati al-ḍabbata wa-fataḥati al-bāba wa-faʿalat hādhihi al-fiʿāla
sentences.l: And-he-informed-him of-(the)-cause (of) his-going-out from his-land and-his-kingdom, and-that-he not entered the-hall by-his-choice, but the-girl, she (is) who broke the-lock and-opened the-door and-did these deeds.
sentences.i: He told him why he had left his land and his kingdom, and that he had not entered the hall of his own free will: it was the girl who had broken the lock, opened the door and done all this.
sentences.n: The print has واله, a misprint for وانه, corrected here: wa-annahu, 'and that he'. akhbara bi-, 'to inform (someone) of': bi- marks the matter, both bi-sababi and the anna-clause. mā dakhala, 'he did not enter', is printed run together, مادخل; kept as set. bi-ikhtiyārihi, 'by his own choice'. hiya allatī, 'she (it is) who', points the blame at her. lākinna takes the accusative, al-ṣabiyyata; it and hādhihi take a dagger alif.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ بَهَادُرُ كَلَامَ الْأَمْجَدِ وَمَاجَرَى عَلَيْهِ وَعَرَفَ أَنَّهُ ابْنُ مَلِكٍ حَنَّ عَلَيْهِ وَرَحِمَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Bahāduru kalāma al-Amjadi wa-mā jarā ʿalayhi wa-ʿarafa annahu ibnu malikin ḥanna ʿalayhi wa-raḥimahu
sentences.l: And-when heard Bahādur (the) speech (of) al-Amjad and-what had-befallen him, and-knew that-he (was the) son (of) a-king, he-felt-tender toward-him and-pitied-him.
sentences.i: When Bahādur heard al-Amjad's words and all that had befallen him, and learned that he was a king's son, his heart went out to him and he took pity on him.
sentences.n: mā jarā ʿalayhi, 'what ran upon him', what befell him; printed run together, وماجرى, kept as set. ḥanna ʿalā, 'to feel tenderness towards': ʿalā marks the one pitied. The shadda of حنّ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ اسْمَعْ يَا أَمْجَدُ كَلَامِي وَأَطِعْنِي وَأَنَا أَتَكَفَّلُ لَكَ بِالْأَمَانِ مِمَّا تَخَافُ وَإِنْ خَالَفْتَنِي قَتَلْتُكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahu ismaʿ yā Amjadu kalāmī wa-aṭiʿnī wa-anā atakaffalu laka bi-al-amāni mimmā takhāfu wa-in khālaftanī qataltuka
sentences.l: Then he-said to-him: Hear, O Amjad, my-speech, and-obey-me, and-I guarantee to-you the-safety from-what you-fear; and-if you-oppose-me, I-kill-you.
sentences.i: Then he said to him, “Listen to me, Amjad, and do as I say, and I will answer for your safety from all you fear; but if you go against me, I will kill you.”
sentences.n: yā Amjadu: the name is addressed without its article, as names of this kind often are in the vocative, and so takes -u. takaffala li- … bi-, 'to stand surety to (someone) for (something)': li- marks the one assured, bi- the thing guaranteed; its shadda is printed. in khālaftanī qataltuka: both verbs of the condition are perfects, with future sense, 'if you oppose me, I will kill you'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ أَذْ مُرْنِي بِمَا شِئْتَ فَأَنَا لَا أُخَالِفُكَ أَبَدًا لِأَنَّنِي عَتِيقُ مُرُوَّتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu adh murnī bi-mā shiʾta fa-anā lā ukhālifuka abadan li-annanī ʿatīqu muruwwatika
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad: [Then?] command-me with-what you-wish, for-I do-not oppose-you ever, because-I (am the) freedman (of) your-chivalry.
sentences.i: “Then command me whatever you wish,” said al-Amjad, “for I will never go against you: I owe my life to your generosity.”
sentences.n: أذ is obscure. It may be a misprint, perhaps for idhan, 'then, in that case', with its nūn lost, which fits the sense; or it may be a stray letter. It is kept as printed and vocalised adh, and read here as 'then', with doubt. murnī, 'command me', is the short imperative of amara, which drops its hamza; amara bi-, 'to order (someone) to do', so bi-mā shiʾta, 'whatever you wish'. ʿatīq, 'a freed slave', so ʿatīqu muruwwatika, 'the freedman of your chivalry': one who owes his life and liberty to your nobility. مروتك is the print's spelling of muruwwa, itself the softened form of muruʾa, 'manliness, chivalry'; vocalised muruwwatika. The shadda of لانّني is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ بَهَادُرُ ادْخُلِ السَّاعَةَ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ وَاجْلِسْ فِى الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي كُنْتَ فِيهِ وَاطْمَئِنَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Bahāduru udkhuli al-sāʿata ilā al-bayti wa-ijlis fī al-makāni alladhī kunta fīhi wa-iṭmaʾinna
sentences.l: And-said to-him Bahādur: Go-in the-hour to the-house and-sit in the-place which you-were in-it, and-be-at-ease.
sentences.i: Bahādur said to him, “Go back into the house this moment, sit where you were sitting, and set your mind at rest.”
sentences.n: al-sāʿata, 'the hour', as an adverb means 'now, at once'. iṭmaʾinna, imperative of iṭmaʾanna, 'to be at rest'; its ئ and shadda are printed. فى is printed with ى; kept as set.

sentences.t: وَهَا أَنَا دَاخِلٌ إِلَيْكَ وَاسْمِي بَهَادُرُ
sentences.tr: wa-hā anā dākhilun ilayka wa-ismī Bahāduru
sentences.l: And-here I (am) coming-in to-you, and-my-name (is) Bahādur.
sentences.i: I will come in to you directly; my name is Bahādur.
sentences.n: hā anā dākhilun, 'here I am, coming in': the participle gives the near future. He tells al-Amjad his name so that he can play the master and call his 'slave' by it.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا دَخَلْتُ إِلَيْكَ فَاشْتِمْنِي وَانْهَرْنِي وَقُلْ لِي مَا سَبَبُ تَأَخُّرِكَ إِلَى هٰذَا الْوَقْتِ وَلَاتَقْبَلْ لِي عُذْرًا بَلْ قُمِ اضْرِبْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-idhā dakhaltu ilayka fa-ishtimnī wa-inharnī wa-qul lī mā sababu taʾakhkhurika ilā hādhā al-waqti wa-lā taqbal lī ʿudhran bal qumi iḍribnī
sentences.l: And-when I-enter to-you, then-revile-me and-rebuke-me, and-say to-me: What (is the) cause (of) your-lateness to this time? And-do-not accept from-me an-excuse, but rise, beat-me.
sentences.i: “When I come in, curse me and scold me, and say to me, ‘Why are you so late?’ Accept no excuse from me, but get up and beat me.”
sentences.n: idhā dakhaltu, 'when I come in': the perfect after idhā refers to the future, and fa- opens the answer. shatama, 'to revile', imperative ishtim; nahara, 'to rebuke, drive off with harsh words', imperative inhar. The damma of دخلتُ and the hamza and shadda of تأخّرك are printed. lā taqbal lī ʿudhran, 'do not accept from me an excuse': li- here marks the one whose excuse it is; printed run together, ولاتقبل, kept as set. qumi iḍribnī, 'rise, beat me': two imperatives side by side, without 'and'.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ شَفَقْتَ عَلَيَّ أَعْدَمْتُكَ حَيٰوتَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-in shafaqta ʿalayya aʿdamtuka ḥayātaka
sentences.l: And-if you-have-pity on-me, I-deprive-you (of) your-life.
sentences.i: “And if you spare me, I will take your life.”
sentences.n: shafaqa ʿalā, 'to feel pity for', where Classical usually has Form IV, ashfaqa ʿalā; the print has the plain verb. The shadda of عليّ is printed. aʿdama, Form IV, 'to make (someone) lose (something)', takes two objects: aʿdamtuka ḥayātaka, 'I will make you lose your life'. حيوتك is the old spelling of ḥayātaka with wāw for the long ā, and takes a dagger alif.

sentences.t: فَادْخُلْ وَانْبَسِطْ وَمَهْمَا طَلَبْتَهُ مِنِّي فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ تَجِدْهُ حَاضِرًا بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ فِى الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-udkhul wa-inbasiṭ wa-mahmā ṭalabtahu minnī fī hādhihi al-sāʿati tajidhu ḥāḍiran bayna yadayka fī al-waqti
sentences.l: So-go-in and-be-merry, and-whatever you-ask-it from-me in this hour you-find-it present between your-two-hands at the-moment.
sentences.i: “Now go in and enjoy yourself. Whatever you ask of me at this hour you will find set before you that instant.”
sentences.n: inbasiṭ, Form VII of b-s-ṭ, 'to be spread out', of a person 'to be at ease, cheerful'. mahmā, 'whatever', takes the perfect in the condition and the jussive in the answer, tajidhu, 'you will find it'. bayna yadayka, 'between your two hands', is 'before you'. fī al-waqti, 'at the time', means 'at once'; فى is printed with ى, kept as set.

sentences.t: وَبِتْ كَمَا تُحِبُّ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَفِي غَدٍ تَوَجَّهْ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِكَ إِكْرَامًا لِغُرْبَتِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-bit kamā tuḥibbu fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-fī ghadin tawajjah ilā ḥāli sabīlika ikrāman li-ghurbatika
sentences.l: And-spend-the-night as you-like in this night, and-on the-morrow betake-yourself to (the) state (of) your-way, (as an) honouring for-your-strangerhood.
sentences.i: “Pass the night as you please, and tomorrow go on your way: I do this in honour of your being a stranger here.”
sentences.n: bit, 'spend the night', the short imperative of bāta. ḥāli sabīlika, 'the state of your way': tawajjah ilā ḥāli sabīlika, 'go off about your business'. ikrāman, an accusative of purpose, 'out of honour'; li-ghurbatika, 'for your strangerhood': li- marks what is honoured. ghurba is being far from home. The shadda of توجّه is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي أُحِبُّ الْغَرِيبَ وَوَاجِبٌ عَلَيَّ إِكْرَامُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-innī uḥibbu al-gharība wa-wājibun ʿalayya ikrāmuhu
sentences.l: For-indeed-I love the-stranger, and-incumbent upon-me (is) honouring-him.
sentences.i: “For I love a stranger, and it is my duty to honour him.”
sentences.n: wājibun ʿalayya, 'incumbent upon me': ʿalā marks the one on whom the duty lies, and the predicate comes first. The shaddas of فانّي and عليّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلَ الْأَمْجَدُ يَدَهُ وَدَخَلَ وَقَدْ إِكْتَسَى وَجْهُهُ حُمْرَةً وَبَيَاضًا
sentences.tr: fa-qabbala al-Amjadu yadahu wa-dakhala wa-qad iktasā wajhuhu ḥumratan wa-bayāḍan
sentences.l: And-kissed al-Amjad his-hand and-went-in, and-had clothed-itself his-face (with) redness and-whiteness.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad kissed his hand and went in, the colour back in his face, red and white.
sentences.n: iktasā, Form VIII of k-s-w, 'to be clothed', with an accusative of what clothes it: his face put on red and white again, the colour of health, after the yellow of fear. The print writes the alif of this verb with a hamza, إكتسى, though it is a connecting alif; kept as set. wa-qad + perfect makes a circumstantial clause, 'his face having taken on'. The shadda of فقبّل is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَوَّلَ مَادَخَلَ قَالَ لِلصَّبِيَّةِ يَاسِتِّي أَنَّسْتِ مَوْضِعَكِ وَهٰذِهِ لَيْلَةٌ مُبَارَكَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-awwala mā dakhala qāla li-al-ṣabiyyati yā sittī annasti mawḍiʿaki wa-hādhihi laylatun mubārakatun
sentences.l: And-first (of) what he-entered, he-said to-the-girl: O-my-lady, you-have-cheered your-place, and-this (is) a-night blessed.
sentences.i: The moment he came in he said to the girl, “My lady, you have brought delight to your own house, and this is a blessed night.”
sentences.n: awwala mā dakhala, 'the first thing (when) he entered', is an adverbial accusative, 'as soon as he came in'; mā dakhala is printed as one word, مادخل. sitt, 'lady', is the later word for sayyida; yā sittī is printed run together, its shadda printed. أنست is read here as annasti, Form II, 'you have cheered, made sociable', the welcome one says to a guest; it may equally be Form IV ānasti, the usual verb of that welcome, its madda left unprinted. Either way he calls the place hers, mawḍiʿaki, 'your place', playing the host's part, where an hour before he sat in it sick with fear.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الصَّبِيَّهُ إِنَّ هٰذَا عَجِيبٌ مِنْكَ حَيْثُ بَسَطْتَ لِي الْأُنْسَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ṣabiyyatu inna hādhā ʿajībun minka ḥaythu basaṭta lī al-unsa
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-girl: Indeed this (is) wonderful from-you, seeing-that you-have-spread for-me the-cheer.
sentences.i: The girl said to him, “Now this is a marvel from you, that you should show me such good cheer!”
sentences.n: She is surprised, after his gloom. basaṭa lahu al-uns, 'to spread out companionship for someone', to be warm and cheerful with him: li- marks the one it is offered to. ḥaythu, 'where', here 'seeing that, in that'. The print writes الصبيه with ه for ة, as it sometimes does; kept as set.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ وَاللّٰهِ يَاسَيِّدَتِي إِنِّي كُنْتُ أَعْتَقِدُأَنَّ مَمْلُوكِي بَهَادُرَ أَخَذَلِي عُقُودَ جَوَاهِرَ كُلُّ عِقْدٍ يُسَاوِى عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu wa-allāhi yā sayyidatī innī kuntu aʿtaqidu anna mamlūkī Bahādura akhadha lī ʿuqūda jawāhira kullu ʿiqdin yusāwī ʿasharata ālāfi dīnārin
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad: By-God, O-my-lady, indeed-I was believing that my-slave Bahādur had-taken from-me necklaces (of) jewels, every necklace is-worth ten thousands (of) dinar.
sentences.i: “By God, my lady,” said al-Amjad, “I had come to believe that my slave Bahādur had stolen some jewelled necklaces of mine, each worth ten thousand dinars.”
sentences.n: He makes up a story to explain his black mood and the slave's lateness. kuntu aʿtaqidu, 'I was believing'. The print runs aʿtaqidu and anna together, اعتقدان, and akhadha and lī together, اخذلي; both are kept as set. akhadha lī, 'took of mine': li- marks the one deprived. ʿuqūda jawāhira, 'necklaces of jewels': jawāhir is a diptote, its genitive -a. kullu ʿiqdin yusāwī …, 'each necklace being worth …', is a clause describing them; يساوى is printed with ى. The madda of آلاف is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّنِي خَرَجْتُ السَّاعَةَ وَأَنَا مُتَفَكِّرٌ فِي ذٰلِكَ فَفَتَّشْتُ عَلَيْهَا فَوَجَدْتُهَا فِي مَوْضِعِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innanī kharajtu al-sāʿata wa-anā mutafakkirun fī dhālika fa-fattashtu ʿalayhā fa-wajadtuhā fī mawḍiʿihā
sentences.l: Then indeed-I went-out the-hour, and-I (was) thinking about that, and-I-searched for-them and-found-them in their-place.
sentences.i: “Just now I went out, still turning the matter over, and searched for them, and found them in their place.”
sentences.n: fattasha ʿalā, 'to search for', with ʿalā marking what is looked for, a later usage. The necklaces, a non-human plural, are referred to with the feminine singular -hā, 'them'.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَدْرِ مَاسَبَبُ تَأَخُّرِ الْمَمْلُوكِ إِلَي هٰذَا الْوَقْتِ وَلَابُدَّلِي مِنْ عُقُوبَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam adri mā sababu taʾakhkhuri al-mamlūki ilā hādhā al-waqti wa-lā budda lī min ʿuqūbatihi
sentences.l: And-not I-know what (is the) cause (of the) lateness (of) the-slave to this time, and-no escape for-me from his-punishment.
sentences.i: “But I do not know why the slave is so late, and I shall have to punish him.”
sentences.n: lam adri, jussive of adrī, 'I do not know'. mā sababu is printed run together, ماسبب; kept as set. الي is the print's spelling of ilā, with ي; kept as set. lā budda lī min, 'there is no escape for me from', 'I must': li- marks the one bound to do it, min the thing that must be done; printed as one word, ولابدلي. The hamza of تأخر is printed.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَرَاحَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ بِكَلَامِ الْأَمْجَدِ
sentences.tr: fa-istarāḥati al-ṣabiyyatu bi-kalāmi al-Amjadi
sentences.l: And-was-eased the-girl by-(the)-speech (of) al-Amjad.
sentences.i: The girl was quite set at ease by what al-Amjad said.
sentences.n: istarāḥa, Form X of r-w-ḥ, 'to find rest, be relieved'; bi-, 'by', of the cause.

sentences.t: وَلَعِبَا وَشَرِبَا وَانْشَرَحَا وَلَمْ يَزَالَا فِي حَظٍّ إِلَى قَرِيبِ الْمَغْرِبِ
sentences.tr: wa-laʿibā wa-sharibā wa-insharaḥā wa-lam yazālā fī ḥaẓẓin ilā qarībi al-maghribi
sentences.l: And-the-two-played and-the-two-drank and-the-two-were-merry, and-not the-two-ceased in pleasure until near the-sunset.
sentences.i: They played and drank and made merry, and went on enjoying themselves until close on sunset.
sentences.n: Duals throughout: laʿibā, sharibā, insharaḥā, 'the two of them played, drank, were glad'. insharaḥa, Form VII, 'to be opened out', of the breast, 'to be glad'. lam yazālā, 'they did not cease', with fī ḥaẓẓin, 'in enjoyment'; the shadda of حظّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهِمَا بَهَادُرُ وَقَدْ غَيَّرَ لِبْسَهُ وَشَدَّ وَسَطَهُ وَجَعَلَ فِي رِجْلَيْهِ زَرْبُونًا عَلَى عَادَةِ الْمَمَالِيكِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala ʿalayhimā Bahāduru wa-qad ghayyara libsahu wa-shadda wasaṭahu wa-jaʿala fī rijlayhi zarbūnan ʿalā ʿādati al-mamālīki
sentences.l: And-came-in upon-the-two Bahādur, and-he-had changed his-clothing and-girded his-middle and-put on his-two-feet a-shoe according-to (the) custom (of) the-mamluks.
sentences.i: Then Bahādur came in to them. He had changed his clothes, girded his waist, and put on his feet the shoes that mamluks wear.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, 'to come in upon, enter the presence of'. He has dressed as a slave in service: libs, 'clothing'; shadda wasaṭahu, 'he tied his middle', girded himself for work. zarbūn, a kind of shoe or slipper of later usage, a word of foreign origin (also zarbūl); its exact form is uncertain. ʿalā ʿādati, 'according to the custom of'. The shaddas of غيّر and شدّ are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَلَّمَ وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ وَكَتَّفَ يَدَيْهِ وَأَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ كَالْمُعْتَرِفِ بِذَنْبِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma sallama wa-qabbala al-arḍa wa-kattafa yadayhi wa-aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi ka-al-muʿtarifi bi-dhanbihi
sentences.l: Then he-greeted and-kissed the-ground and-folded his-two-hands and-bowed with-his-head to the-ground, like-the-one-confessing his-sin.
sentences.i: He gave the greeting, kissed the ground, folded his arms, and hung his head towards the floor like a man who owns his fault.
sentences.n: kattafa yadayhi, Form II, 'to fold one's arms (across the chest)', the posture of a servant standing ready; its shadda is printed, as are those of سلّم and قبّل. aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi, 'to lower the head', in shame. ka-al-muʿtarifi, 'like the confessing one': ka-, 'like'; iʿtarafa bi-, 'to confess': bi- marks what is confessed. The hamza of برأسه is printed.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ الْأَمْجَدُ بِعَيْنِ الْغَضَبِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا أَنْحَسَ الْمَمَالِيكِ مَاسَبَبُ تَأَخُّرِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ilayhi al-Amjadu bi-ʿayni al-ghaḍabi wa-qāla lahu yā anḥasa al-mamālīki mā sababu taʾakhkhurika
sentences.l: And-looked at-him al-Amjad with-(the)-eye (of) the-anger and-said to-him: O most-ill-omened (of) the-mamluks, what (is the) cause (of) your-lateness?
sentences.i: Al-Amjad gave him an angry look and said to him, “You most ill-starred of slaves, why are you so late?”
sentences.n: yā anḥasa al-mamālīki, 'O most ill-omened of the mamluks': the elative is annexed to the group, 'the worst of'. mā sababu is printed as one word, ماسبب; the hamza and shadda of تأخّرك are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي إِنِّي اشْتَغَلْتُ بِغَسْلِ أَثْوَابِي وَمَا عَلِمْتُ أَنَّكَ هَاهُنَا لِأَنَّ مِيعَادِي وَمِيعَادَكَ الْعِشَاءُ لَابِالنَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī innī ishtaghaltu bi-ghasli athwābī wa-mā ʿalimtu annaka hāhunā li-anna mīʿādī wa-mīʿādaka al-ʿishāʾu lā bi-al-nahāri
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: O-my-lord, indeed-I was-busied with-(the)-washing (of) my-clothes, and-not I-knew that-you (were) here, because my-appointment and-your-appointment (is) the-evening, not by-the-day.
sentences.i: “My lord,” he answered, “I was busy washing my clothes, and I did not know you were here, for our appointed time is nightfall, not the daytime.”
sentences.n: ishtaghala bi-, 'to be busy with': bi- names the work. mīʿād, 'appointed time'. lā bi-al-nahāri, 'not by day': bi- of time, 'in, during'; printed as one word, لابالنهار, kept as set.

sentences.t: فَصَرَخَ عَلَيْهِ الْأَمْجَدُ وَقَالَ لَهُ تَكْذِبُ يَا أَنْحَسَ الْمَمَالِيكِ وَاللّٰهِ لَابُدَّ مِنْ ضَرْبِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣarakha ʿalayhi al-Amjadu wa-qāla lahu takdhibu yā anḥasa al-mamālīki wa-allāhi lā budda min ḍarbika
sentences.l: And-shouted at-him al-Amjad and-said to-him: You-lie, O most-ill-omened (of) the-mamluks! By-God, no escape from your-beating.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad shouted at him, “You are lying, you wretch of a slave! By God, you shall have a beating!”
sentences.n: ṣarakha ʿalā, 'to shout at': ʿalā marks the one shouted at. lā budda min ḍarbika, 'there is no escape from beating you': ḍarbika is a verbal noun with its object as the suffix. The shadda of لابدّ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ الْأَمْجَدُ وَسَطَحَ بَهَادُرَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ وَأَخَذَ عَصًا وَضَرَبَهُ بِرِفْقٍ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma al-Amjadu wa-saṭaḥa Bahādura ʿalā al-arḍi wa-akhadha ʿaṣan wa-ḍarabahu bi-rifqin
sentences.l: Then rose al-Amjad and-laid-flat Bahādur on the-ground, and-took a-stick and-beat-him with-gentleness.
sentences.i: Then al-Amjad got up, laid Bahādur flat on the floor, took a stick and beat him, gently.
sentences.n: saṭaḥa, 'to spread out flat, throw (someone) down on his back' (Lane). bi-rifqin, 'with gentleness': bi- of manner.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَخَلَّصَتِ الْعَصَا مِنْ يَدَيْهِ وَنَزَلَتْ عَلَي بَهَادُرَ بِضَرْبٍ وَجِيعٍ حَتَّى آلَمَهُ الضَّرْبُ وَجَرَتْ دُمُوعُهُ وَاسْتَغَاثَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmati al-ṣabiyyatu wa-khallaṣati al-ʿaṣā min yadayhi wa-nazalat ʿalā Bahādura bi-ḍarbin wajīʿin ḥattā ālamahu al-ḍarbu wa-jarat dumūʿuhu wa-istaghātha
sentences.l: And-rose the-girl and-wrested the-stick from his-two-hands and-came-down upon Bahādur with-a-beating painful, until hurt-him the-beating and-ran his-tears and-he-cried-for-help.
sentences.i: At that the girl got up, wrenched the stick from his hands, and fell upon Bahādur with a cruel beating, until the blows hurt him and his tears ran and he cried out for help.
sentences.n: The print has آلمة, a misprint for آلمه, corrected here: ālamahu, 'it hurt him', with the madda printed. khallaṣa min, 'to free (something) from', here 'to wrest away from'; the shaddas of الصبيّة and خلّصت are printed. nazala ʿalā … bi-, 'to come down upon (someone) with': ʿalā marks the victim, bi- what she lays on. علي is printed with ي for ʿalā; kept as set. istaghātha, Form X of gh-w-th, 'to call for help'.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ يَكُزُّ عَلَى أَسْنَانِهِ وَالْأَمْجَدُ يَصِيحُ عَلَى الصَّبِيَّةِ لَا تَفْعَلِي وَهِيَ تَقُولُ دَعْنِي أَشْتَفِي غَيْظِي مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra yakuzzu ʿalā asnānihi wa-al-Amjadu yaṣīḥu ʿalā al-ṣabiyyati lā tafʿalī wa-hiya taqūlu daʿnī ashtafī ghayẓī minhu
sentences.l: And-he-became clenching on his-teeth, while-al-Amjad cries at the-girl: Do-not do (it)! and-she says: Let-me I-satisfy my-rage from-him.
sentences.i: He took to gritting his teeth, while al-Amjad shouted at the girl, “Stop that!” and she kept saying, “Let me take out my anger on him!”
sentences.n: ṣāra yakuzzu, 'he took to clenching': kazza ʿalā asnānihi, 'to clamp the teeth together', in pain; its shadda is printed. yaṣīḥu ʿalā, 'to cry out at': ʿalā marks the one shouted at. lā tafʿalī, 'do not do (so)!', prohibitive jussive. ashtafī ghayẓī minhu, 'that I may heal my rage from him': ishtafā, Form VIII of sh-f-y, 'to be cured', of rage 'to vent it on, have satisfaction of'; min marks the one on whom it is vented. After daʿnī Classical wants the jussive ashtafi, without the final ī; the print has the indicative, as later Arabic does, and it is read so.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْأَمْجَدَ خَطَفَ الْعَصَا مِنْ يَدِهَا وَدَفَعَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-Amjada khaṭafa al-ʿaṣā min yadihā wa-dafaʿahā
sentences.l: Then indeed al-Amjad snatched the-stick from her-hand and-pushed-her (away).
sentences.i: Then al-Amjad snatched the stick out of her hand and pushed her aside.
sentences.n: khaṭafa, 'to snatch'. dafaʿahā, 'he pushed her (away)'.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ بَهَادُرُ وَمَسَحَ دُمُوعَهُ مِنْ وَجْهِهِ وَوَقَفَ فِي خِدْمَتِهِمَا سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāma Bahāduru wa-masaḥa dumūʿahu min wajhihi wa-waqafa fī khidmatihimā sāʿatan
sentences.l: And-rose Bahādur and-wiped his-tears from his-face, and-stood in their-service an-hour.
sentences.i: Bahādur got up, wiped the tears from his face, and stood waiting on them for a while.
sentences.n: waqafa fī khidmatihimā, 'he stood in the service of the two of them', stood by to wait on them. sāʿatan, 'an hour', here simply 'a while', accusative of duration.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَسَحَ الْقَاعَةَ وَأَوْقَدَ الْقَنَادِيلَ
sentences.tr: thumma masaḥa al-qāʿata wa-awqada al-qanādīla
sentences.l: Then he-wiped the-hall and-lit the-lamps.
sentences.i: Then he swept the hall and lit the lamps.
sentences.n: masaḥa, 'to wipe', here 'to clean' the floor of the hall. awqada, Form IV, 'to kindle'; qanādīl, plural of qindīl, 'lamp', from Greek through Aramaic.

sentences.t: وَصَارَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ كُلَّ مَا خَرَجَ أَوْدَخَلَ بَهَادُرُ تَشْتُمُهُ وَتَلْعَنُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārati al-ṣabiyyatu kulla mā kharaja aw dakhala Bahāduru tashtumuhu wa-talʿanuhu
sentences.l: And-took-to the-girl, every-time (that) went-out or-came-in Bahādur, reviling-him and-cursing-him.
sentences.i: And every time Bahādur went out or came in, the girl would revile him and curse him.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, 'to take to, begin to': the habit is in the imperfects tashtumuhu wa-talʿanuhu. كل ما, written as two words, is the edition's spelling of kullamā, 'whenever'. The print runs aw dakhala, 'or came in', together as اودخل; it is kept as set. The shadda of الصبيّة is printed.

sentences.t: وَالْأَمْجَدُ يَغْضَبُ مِنْهَا وَيَقُولُ لَهَا بِحَقِّ اللّٰهِ تَعَالَى عَلَيْكِ أَنْ تَتْرُكِي مَمْلُوكِي فَإِنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُعَوَّدٍ بِهٰذَا
sentences.tr: wa-al-Amjadu yaghḍabu minhā wa-yaqūlu lahā bi-ḥaqqi Allāhi taʿālā ʿalayki an tatrukī mamlūkī fa-innahu ghayru muʿawwadin bi-hādhā
sentences.l: And-al-Amjad grows-angry from-her and-says to-her: By-(the)-right (of) God (the) Exalted upon-you, that you-leave my-slave, for-indeed-he (is) not accustomed to-this.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad would grow angry with her and say to her, “By God the Exalted, I beg you, leave my slave alone; he is not used to this.”
sentences.n: wa-al-Amjadu yaghḍabu, 'while al-Amjad would grow angry', a circumstantial clause; the imperfects tell what happened again and again. ghaḍiba min, 'to be angry at': min marks the cause. bi-ḥaqqi Allāhi ʿalayki, 'by God's claim upon you', is an adjuration, and the an-clause with the subjunctive tatrukī says what is begged. Al-Amjad keeps up the pretence that Bahādur is his slave. muʿawwad bi-, 'accustomed to': bi- marks the thing one is used to; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمَا لَمْ يَزَالَا يَأْكُلَانِ وَيَشْرَبَانِ وَبَهَادُرُ فِي خِدْمَتِهِمَا إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ حَتَّى تَعِبَ مِنَ الْخِدْمَةِ وَالضَّرْبِ فَنَامَ فِي وَسْطِ الْقَاعَةِ وَشَخَرَ وَنَخَرَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahumā lam yazālā yaʾkulāni wa-yashrabāni wa-Bahāduru fī khidmatihimā ilā niṣfi al-layli ḥattā taʿiba mina al-khidmati wa-al-ḍarbi fa-nāma fī wasṭi al-qāʿati wa-shakhara wa-nakhara
sentences.l: Then indeed-the-two did-not cease eating and-drinking, and-Bahādur (was) in their-service, to (the) half (of) the-night, until he-tired from the-service and-the-beating, and-he-slept in (the) middle (of) the-hall and-snored and-snorted.
sentences.i: So the two of them went on eating and drinking, with Bahādur waiting on them, until midnight, when he was worn out with serving and with being beaten; and he fell asleep in the middle of the hall, snoring and snorting.
sentences.n: thumma innahumā, 'then the two of them': thumma inna is the story's usual way of opening the next step, and the inna adds no special emphasis. lam yazālā with an imperfect, 'they did not cease to', so 'they kept on'. wa-Bahāduru fī khidmatihimā is a circumstantial clause. The ء of يأكلان is printed. shakhara wa-nakhara, a jingling pair: shakhara is to snore, nakhara to snort through the nose.

sentences.t: فَسَكِرَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَقَالَتْ لِلْأَمْجَدِ قُمْ خُذْ هٰذَا السَّيْفَ الْمُعَلَّقَ وَاضْرِبْ رَقَبَةَ هٰذَا الْمَمْلُوكِ وَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ عَمِلْتُ عَلَى هَلَاكِ رُوحِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-sakirati al-ṣabiyyatu wa-qālat li-al-Amjadi qum khudh hādhā al-sayfa al-muʿallaqa wa-iḍrib raqabata hādhā al-mamlūki wa-in lam tafʿal ʿamiltu ʿalā halāki rūḥika
sentences.l: And-became-drunk the-girl and-said to-al-Amjad: Rise, take this the-sword the-hung and-strike (the) neck (of) this the-slave; and-if you-do-not do (it), I-work toward (the) destruction (of) your-soul.
sentences.i: The girl grew drunk, and she said to al-Amjad, “Get up, take this sword that hangs here, and strike off this slave's head. If you will not, I will see to it that you lose your own life.”
sentences.n: qum khudh, 'get up, take', two imperatives without wa-, as in speech. al-muʿallaq, 'hung up', of the sword hanging on the wall; its shadda is printed. ḍaraba raqabatahu, 'to strike his neck', is to behead. In the answer of a condition the perfect ʿamiltu looks forward: 'I will work for'. ʿamila ʿalā, 'to work toward, set about': ʿalā marks the aim. rūḥ, 'soul, life'; halāk rūḥika is 'your own death'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ خَطَرَ لَكِ فِي قَتْلِ مَمْلُوكِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu wa-ayyu shayʾin khaṭara laki fī qatli mamlūkī
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad: And-what thing occurred to-you in (the) killing (of) my-slave?
sentences.i: “And what has put it into your head to kill my slave?” said al-Amjad.
sentences.n: The same khaṭara li- as when she broke the lock: li- marks the one in whose mind a thought arises; fī, 'about, as to'. The shadda of ايّ and the ء of شيء are printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ لَايَكْمُلُ الْحَظُّ إِلَّا بِقَتْلِهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ تَقُمْ قُمْتُ أَنَا وَقَتَلْتُهُ
sentences.tr: qālat lā yakmulu al-ḥaẓẓu illā bi-qatlihi wa-in lam taqum qumtu anā wa-qataltuhu
sentences.l: She-said: Not-is-complete the-pleasure except by-killing-him; and-if you-do-not rise, I-rise, I, and-I-kill-him.
sentences.i: “Our pleasure will never be complete unless he is killed,” she said. “If you will not get up, I will get up myself and kill him.”
sentences.n: The print runs lā yakmulu together as لايكمل; kept as set. al-ḥaẓẓ is here 'pleasure, enjoyment', the word used of the hall Bahādur fitted out li-ḥaẓẓihi; its shadda is printed, as is that of الّا. bi-qatlihi: bi-, 'by means of'. qumtu … wa-qataltuhu, perfects looking forward in the answer of the condition; anā stresses 'I myself'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ بِحَقِّ اللّٰهِ عَلَيْكِ لَا تَفْعَلِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu bi-ḥaqqi Allāhi ʿalayki lā tafʿalī
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad: By-(the)-right (of) God upon-you, do-not do (it)!
sentences.i: “By God, I beg you,” said al-Amjad, “do not do it!”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَابُدَّ مِنْ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lā budda min hādhā
sentences.l: And-she-said: No-escape from this.
sentences.i: “There is no help for it,” she said.
sentences.n: lā budda min, 'there is no escape from': min marks what cannot be avoided. The print sets it as one word, لابد.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَتِ السَّيْفَ وَجَرَّدَتْهُ وَهَمَّتْ بِقَتْلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhati al-sayfa wa-jarradathu wa-hammat bi-qatlihi
sentences.l: And-she-took the-sword and-bared-it and-was-about-to killing-him.
sentences.i: She took the sword, drew it, and was on the point of killing him.
sentences.n: jarrada, 'to strip', of a sword 'to draw it from the sheath'. hamma bi-, 'to be about to, set about': the verb chooses bi- for the deed intended. Both shaddas are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ فِي نَفْسِهِ هٰذَا رَجُلٌ عَمِلَ مَعَنَا خَيْرًا وَسَتَرَنَا وَأَحْسَنَ إِلَيْنَا وَجَعَلَ نَفْسَهُ مَمْلُوكِي كَيْفَ نُجَازِيهِ بِالْقَتْلِ لَاكَانَ ذٰلِكَ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu fī nafsihi hādhā rajulun ʿamila maʿanā khayran wa-sataranā wa-aḥsana ilaynā wa-jaʿala nafsahu mamlūkī kayfa nujāzīhi bi-al-qatli lā kāna dhālika abadan
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad in himself: This (is) a-man (who) did with-us good and-covered-us and-did-well to-us and-made himself my-slave; how (shall) we-repay-him with-the-killing? May-not-be that ever!
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said to himself, “Here is a man who has done us a kindness, kept our secret and treated us well, and has made himself my slave. How can we repay him by killing him? That shall never be!”
sentences.n: ʿamila maʿahu khayran, 'to do someone a good turn': maʿa marks the one treated. satara, 'to cover', here 'to shield from exposure': he did not give them away. aḥsana ilā, 'to do good to': ilā marks the one who benefits. jāzā bi-, 'to repay with': bi- marks what the repayment is. lā kāna dhālika, printed with lā and kāna run together, is lā with the perfect in a wish: 'may that never be'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِلصَّبِيَّةِ إِنْ كَانَ وَلَابُدَّ مِنْ قَتْلِ مَمْلُوكِي فَأَنَا أَحَقُّ بِقَتْلِهِ مِنْكِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla li-al-ṣabiyyati in kāna wa-lā budda min qatli mamlūkī fa-anā aḥaqqu bi-qatlihi minki
sentences.l: Then he-said to-the-girl: If it-is, and-no-escape from (the) killing (of) my-slave, then-I (am) more-entitled to-killing-him than-you.
sentences.i: Then he said to the girl, “If my slave must needs be killed, I have more right to kill him than you.”
sentences.n: in kāna wa-lā budda, 'if it must be', a set phrase: kāna is impersonal and wa-lā budda a circumstantial clause, 'there being no escape'; ولابد is printed as one word. aḥaqqu bi-, 'more entitled to': bi- marks what one has a right to, and min marks the one compared, 'than you'. The shaddas of الصبيّة and احقّ are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَ السَّيْفَ مِنْ يَدِهَا وَرَفَعَ يَدَهُ وَضَرَبَ الصَّبِيَّةَ فِي عُنُقِهَا فَأَطَاحَ رَأْسَهَا عَنْ جُثَّتِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma akhadha al-sayfa min yadihā wa-rafaʿa yadahu wa-ḍaraba al-ṣabiyyata fī ʿunuqihā fa-aṭāḥa raʾsahā ʿan juththatihā
sentences.l: Then he-took the-sword from her-hand and-raised his-hand and-struck the-girl in her-neck, and-made-fly her-head from her-body.
sentences.i: Then he took the sword from her hand, raised his arm, and struck the girl on the neck, and sent her head flying from her body.
sentences.n: The print has يدة, a misprint for يده, corrected here. aṭāḥa, Form IV of ṭ-y-ḥ, 'to make fall, send flying'; ʿan, 'away from'. The ء of رأسها and the shaddas of الصبيّة and جثّتها are printed.

sentences.t: فَوَقَعَتْ رَأْسُهَا عَلَى صَاحِبِ الدَّارِ فَاسْتَيْقَظَ وَجَلَسَ وَفَتَحَ عَيْنَيْهِ فَوَجَدَ الْأَمْجَدَ وَاقِفًا وَالسَّيْفُ فِي يَدِهِ مُخَضَّبًا بِالدَّمِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqaʿat raʾsuhā ʿalā ṣāḥibi al-dāri fa-istayqaẓa wa-jalasa wa-fataḥa ʿaynayhi fa-wajada al-Amjada wāqifan wa-al-sayfu fī yadihi mukhaḍḍaban bi-al-dami
sentences.l: And-fell her-head upon (the) owner (of) the-house, and-he-woke and-sat and-opened his-eyes, and-found al-Amjad standing, and-the-sword in his-hand, dyed with-the-blood.
sentences.i: Her head fell on the master of the house. He woke, sat up and opened his eyes, and found al-Amjad standing with the sword in his hand, dyed with blood.
sentences.n: The print has يدة, a misprint for يده, corrected here. waqaʿat is feminine, although raʾs, 'head', is normally masculine; it is kept as the text has it. wa-al-sayfu fī yadihi, 'with the sword in his hand', is a circumstantial clause, and mukhaḍḍaban, 'dyed' (khaḍḍaba, Form II, to dye, as with henna), a further accusative of state describing the sword. bi-al-dami: bi- marks what it is dyed with. The shadda of مخضّبا is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ إِلَى الصَّبِيَّةِ فَوَجَدَهَا مَقْتُولَةً فَاسْتَخْبَرَهُ عَنْ أَمْرِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma naẓara ilā al-ṣabiyyati fa-wajadahā maqtūlatan fa-istakhbarahu ʿan amrihā
sentences.l: Then he-looked at the-girl and-found-her killed, and-he-asked-him-for-news about her-affair.
sentences.i: Then he looked at the girl and found her slain, and he asked al-Amjad what had happened with her.
sentences.n: istakhbara, Form X of kh-b-r, 'to ask for news'; ʿan, 'about'.

sentences.t: فَأَعَادَ عَلَيْهِ حَدِيثَهَا وَقَالَ إِنَّهَا أَبَتْ إِلَّا أَنْ تَقْتُلَكَ وَهٰذَا جَزَاؤُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-aʿāda ʿalayhi ḥadīthahā wa-qāla innahā abat illā an taqtulaka wa-hādhā jazāʾuhā
sentences.l: And-he-repeated to-him her-story and-said: Indeed-she refused except that she-kill-you, and-this (is) her-recompense.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad went over the whole story for him and said, “She would have nothing but your death, and this is her reward.”
sentences.n: aʿāda ʿalayhi al-ḥadītha, 'to go over the story for him': ʿalā marks the hearer. abā illā an, 'to refuse anything but that', so 'to insist on'. The ؤ of جزاؤها and the shadda of الّا are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ بَهَادُرُ وَقَبَّلَ رَأْسَ الْأَمْجَدِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي لَيْتَكَ عَفَوْتَ عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāma Bahāduru wa-qabbala raʾsa al-Amjadi wa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī laytaka ʿafawta ʿanhā
sentences.l: And-rose Bahādur and-kissed (the) head (of) al-Amjad and-said to-him: O-my-lord, would-that-you had-pardoned (from) her!
sentences.i: Bahādur rose, kissed al-Amjad's head, and said to him, “My lord, if only you had pardoned her!
sentences.n: Kissing the head is a gesture of thanks and deference. layta with a perfect wishes for what can no longer be. ʿafā ʿan, 'to pardon': ʿan marks the one pardoned. The shadda of قبّل and the ء of رأس are printed.

sentences.t: وَمَابَقِيَ فِى الْأَمْرِ إِلَّا إِخْرَاجُهَا فِي هٰذَا الْوَقْتِ قَبْلَ الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā baqiya fī al-amri illā ikhrājuhā fī hādhā al-waqti qabla al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And-not-remained in the-matter except taking-her-out in this the-time before the-morning.
sentences.i: Now nothing remains but to get her out of here this very hour, before morning.”
sentences.n: mā … illā, 'nothing … but'; ikhrājuhā, 'getting her out', a verbal noun with its object suffix, is the subject of baqiya. ومابقي is printed as one word, and فى with a dotless ى, as often.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ بَهَادُرَ شَدَّ وَسَطَهُ وَأَخَذَ الصَّبِيَّةَ وَلَفَّهَا فِي عَبَاوَةٍ وَوَضَعَهَا فِي فَرْدٍ وَحَمَلَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna Bahādura shadda wasaṭahu wa-akhadha al-ṣabiyyata wa-laffahā fī ʿabāwatin wa-waḍaʿahā fī fardin wa-ḥamalahā
sentences.l: Then indeed Bahādur bound his-middle and-took the-girl and-wrapped-her in a-cloak and-put-her in a-bale and-carried-her.
sentences.i: Then Bahādur girded himself, took the girl, wrapped her in a cloak, put her in a sack and lifted her up.
sentences.n: shadda wasaṭahu, 'he bound his middle', girding up his clothes for work. ʿabāwa is the print's spelling of ʿabāʾa, the wide woollen cloak, with w where the hamza stands; kept as set. fard: Lane gives it as one of a pair of loads slung on either side of a beast, and in later usage a bale or sack; it is masculine here (fīhi below). The shaddas of شدّ and لفّها are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِلْأَمْجَدِ أَنْتَ غَرِيبٌ وَلَا تَعْرِفُ أَحَدًا فَاجْلِسْ فِي مَكَانِكَ وَانْتَظِرْنِي إِلَى وَقْتِ الْفَجْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla li-al-Amjadi anta gharībun wa-lā taʿrifu aḥadan fa-ijlis fī makānika wa-intaẓirnī ilā waqti al-fajri
sentences.l: And-he-said to-al-Amjad: You (are) a-stranger and-not you-know anyone, so-sit in your-place and-wait-for-me until (the) time (of) the-dawn.
sentences.i: And he said to al-Amjad, “You are a stranger here and know no one, so stay where you are and wait for me until dawn.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ عُدْتُ إِلَيْكَ لَا بُدَّ إِنْ أَفْعَلَ مَعَكَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا وَأَجْتَهِدَ فِي كَشْفِ خَبَرِ أَخِيكَ
sentences.tr: fa-in ʿudtu ilayka lā budda in afʿala maʿaka khayran kathīran wa-ajtahida fī kashfi khabari akhīka
sentences.l: And-if I-return to-you, no escape that I-do with-you good much and-strive in uncovering (the) news (of) your-brother.
sentences.i: If I come back to you, I shall surely do you a great kindness and do my utmost to find out what has become of your brother.
sentences.n: The answer to the condition, lā budda, comes without the fa- that Classical Arabic requires before it, a Middle Arabic habit. The print has إن, with its hamza below, where lā budda wants an, 'that'; it is kept as printed, and the verbs after it are read as subjunctives, afʿala and ajtahida, as an would have them. faʿala maʿahu khayran, 'to do someone a good turn': maʿa marks the one treated. ijtahada fī, 'to strive at': fī marks the task.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ وَلَمْ أَعُدْ إِلَيْكَ فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ قَدْقُضِيَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-in ṭalaʿati al-shamsu wa-lam aʿud ilayka fa-iʿlam annahu qad quḍiya ʿalayya
sentences.l: And-if rose the-sun and-not I-returned to-you, then-know that-it has-been-decreed against-me.
sentences.i: But if the sun rises and I have not come back to you, know that my end has come upon me.
sentences.n: quḍiya ʿalā, passive, 'it has been decreed against (someone)', that is, his fate is sealed; the -hu of annahu is the pronoun of the matter, 'that it is so: …'. قدقضي is printed as one word. The hamza of وإن and the shadda of عليّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ وَهٰذِهِ الدَّارُ لَكَ وَلَكَ مَا فِيهَا مِنَ الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْقُمَاشِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-salāmu ʿalayka wa-hādhihi al-dāru laka wa-laka mā fīhā mina al-amwāli wa-al-qumāshi
sentences.l: And-the-peace (be) upon-you; and-this the-house (is) for-you, and-for-you (is) what (is) in-it of the-wealth and-the-stuffs.
sentences.i: Peace be with you. This house is yours, and yours is all that is in it, money and goods alike.”
sentences.n: The print has هذة, a misprint for هذه, corrected here. wa-al-salāmu ʿalayka, a farewell. laka, li- of possession, 'yours'; min after mā spells out what is meant, 'in the way of'. qumāsh, cloth, stuffs, household goods.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ حَمَلَ الْفَرْدَ وَخَرَجَ مِنَ الْقَاعَةِ وَشَقَّ بِهَا الْأَسْوَاقَ وَتَّصَلَ بِهَا طَرِيقَ الْبَحْرِ الْمَالِحِ لِيَرْمِيَهَا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu ḥamala al-farda wa-kharaja mina al-qāʿati wa-shaqqa bihā al-aswāqa wa-ttaṣala bihā ṭarīqa al-baḥri al-māliḥi li-yarmiyahā fīhi
sentences.l: Then indeed-he carried the-bale and-went-out from the-hall and-cut with-her (through) the-markets and-reached with-her (the) road (of) the-sea the-salt, to-throw-her in-it.
sentences.i: Then he shouldered the sack, left the hall, carried her through the markets and came out on the road to the salt sea, to throw her into it.
sentences.n: shaqqa al-aswāqa, 'to cut through the markets'. In bihā, 'with her', bi- marks what one carries along; the feminine is the dead girl, not the masculine fard. وتصل is doubtful. It is read here as wa-ttaṣala, the print's spelling of wa-ittaṣala, 'and he got as far as', with the alif of Form VIII lost as it is in speech; it may as well be a slip for wa-waṣala, 'and he reached', and either way ṭarīq is the place reached. li-yarmiyahā: li- of purpose with the subjunctive. The shadda of شقّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارَ قَرِيبًا مِنَ الْبَحْرِ الْتَفَتَ فَرَأَى بِالْوَالِي وَالْمُقَدَّمِينَ قَدْ أَحَاطُوابِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣāra qarīban mina al-baḥri iltafata fa-raʾā bi-al-wālī wa-al-muqaddamīna qad aḥāṭū bihi
sentences.l: And-when he-became near to the-sea, he-turned and-saw — the-governor and-the-officers had surrounded-him.
sentences.i: When he was close to the sea he looked round, and saw that the chief of police and his captains had surrounded him.
sentences.n: raʾā bi-: the bi- is that of wa-idhā bi-, 'and behold', carried over to raʾā; it only marks what comes into view. al-wālī, the governor of the city, who in these tales keeps order as its chief of police; al-muqaddamūn are his officers, the captains of the watch. aḥāṭa bi-, 'to surround': the verb takes bi- for what is surrounded; احاطوابه is printed as one word. The hamza of فرأى is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا عَرَفُوهُ تَعَجَّبُوا وَفَتَحُوا الْفَرْدَ فَوَجَدُوا فِيهِ قَتِيلَةً
sentences.tr: wa-lammā ʿarafūhu taʿajjabū wa-fataḥū al-farda fa-wajadū fīhi qatīlatan
sentences.l: And-when they-knew-him they-marvelled, and-they-opened the-bale and-found in-it a-slain-woman.
sentences.i: When they recognised him they were astonished; and they opened the sack and found in it a murdered woman.
sentences.n: They are astonished because they know him for the king's master of the horse. qatīla, 'a slain woman', feminine of qatīl. The shadda of تعجّبوا is printed.

sentences.t: فَمَسَكُوهُ وَبَيَّتُوهُ فِى الْحَدِيدِ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-masakūhu wa-bayyatūhu fī al-ḥadīdi ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And-they-seized-him and-made-him-pass-the-night in the-iron until the-morning.
sentences.i: They seized him and kept him in irons through the night until morning.
sentences.n: masaka, Middle Arabic for amsaka, 'to seize'. bayyata, Form II of b-y-t, 'to make (someone) pass the night'; its shadda is printed. fī al-ḥadīd, 'in the iron', in chains.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَلَعُوابِهِ هُوَ وَالْفَرْدُ عَلَى حَالِهِ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ وَأَعْلَمُوهُ بِالْخَبَرِ
sentences.tr: thumma ṭalaʿū bihi huwa wa-al-fardu ʿalā ḥālihi ilā al-maliki wa-aʿlamūhu bi-al-khabari
sentences.l: Then they-went-up with-him, he and-the-bale on its-state, to the-king, and-informed-him of-the-news.
sentences.i: Then they brought him up before the king, him and the sack just as it was, and told the king what had happened.
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa bi-, 'to go up with', so 'to bring (someone) up' to the palace: bi- marks the one taken along; طلعوابه is printed as one word. huwa wa-al-fardu, in the nominative, restates the -hi of bihi and adds the sack to it, a loose Middle Arabic apposition. ʿalā ḥālihi, 'in its state', untouched. aʿlama bi-, 'to inform of': the verb takes bi- for the matter.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمَلِكُ ذٰلِكَ غَضِبَ غَضَبًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-maliku dhālika ghaḍiba ghaḍaban shadīdan
sentences.l: And-when saw the-king that, he-was-angry an-anger severe.
sentences.i: When the king saw this he flew into a violent rage.
sentences.n: راى is printed without its hamza, as the edition often does. ghaḍiba ghaḍaban shadīdan, 'he raged a severe rage', the cognate accusative that intensifies the verb.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ إِنَّكَ تَفْعَلُ هٰكَذَا دَائِمًا فَتَقْتُلُ الْقَتْلَى وَتَرْمِيهِمْ فِى الْبَحْرِ وَتَأْخُذُ جَمِيعَ مَالِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu waylaka innaka tafʿalu hākadhā dāʾiman fa-taqtulu al-qatlā wa-tarmīhim fī al-baḥri wa-taʾkhudhu jamīʿa mālihim
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Woe-to-you! Indeed-you do thus always: and-you-kill the-slain and-throw-them in the-sea and-take all their-wealth.
sentences.i: “Woe to you!” he said to him. “So this is what you are forever doing: you kill your victims and throw them into the sea and take everything they have!
sentences.n: waylaka, 'woe to you', an imprecation. taqtulu al-qatlā, 'you kill the slain', a cognate turn for 'you do people to death'; qatlā is invariable, here the object. The ئ of دائما and the أ of تأخذ are printed; فى as often.

sentences.t: وَكَمْ فَعَلْتَ قَبْلَ ذٰلِكَ مِنْ قَتْلٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kam faʿalta qabla dhālika min qatlin
sentences.l: And-how-many you-did before that of killing!
sentences.i: And how many killings have you done before this!”
sentences.n: kam … min, exclamatory 'how many …!': min names what is counted.

sentences.t: فَأَطْرَقَ بَهَادُرُ رَأْسَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭraqa Bahāduru raʾsahu
sentences.l: And-lowered Bahādur his-head.
sentences.i: Bahādur hung his head.
sentences.n: aṭraqa, Form IV, to bow the head and keep silent. The ء of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print splits the name across a line-end here, شهر / زاد; it is kept as two words.
